Chapter 6. The Fallacy of “Saving” Industries and Jobs.
Let’s dive into an idea that comes up a lot—especially in tough economic times. People often feel a real urge to “save” certain industries or protect jobs when companies start to struggle. It’s a natural reaction, right? Nobody wants to see factories close or friends and neighbors lose their livelihoods.
But here’s something we need to think about. When the government steps in—maybe with tariffs, subsidies, or even big bailouts—to prop up a declining industry, there’s more going on than meets the eye. Sure, it might feel like we’re helping in the moment, keeping some jobs safe. But what about the bigger picture?
The heart of the matter is this: economies aren’t fixed in place. They’re always changing. Industries grow and fade away as technology moves forward, tastes shift, and global competition heats up. If we try to shield an industry from all that change, we might actually be getting in the way of progress.
Let’s look at a few key points that come up whenever we talk about “protecting” certain industries.
First, when you shield an industry from competition, something predictable happens. There’s less pressure to innovate or cut costs. That industry can become inefficient, maybe even a little complacent. Over time, it falls behind instead of getting stronger.
Next, think about where the money for those subsidies or bailouts comes from. It doesn’t just appear out of nowhere. Every dollar spent propping up a declining sector is a dollar that could have gone somewhere else—maybe into new, fast-growing industries that could offer more jobs and better pay down the road.
And don’t forget about consumers. Whenever an industry is protected, prices usually go up. That means everyone has to pay more for those goods, leaving them with less to spend on other things they might need or want.
Let’s bring this to life with a real-world example. Think about when governments step in to protect domestic steel or textile industries. Sure, this can keep a few factories running and some jobs intact. But at the same time, businesses that rely on steel or textiles now have to pay higher prices for their materials. That makes them less competitive, both at home and abroad. And over the long haul, the whole economy can slow down and lose its edge.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? Economic progress depends on letting resources—like money, skills, and talent—move to where they’re needed most. When we try to freeze everything in place, or hold on to every single job just because it exists, we actually limit growth and opportunity for everyone.
It’s tough to see change happening, especially when it affects real people and communities. But giving our economy the freedom to adapt is what helps us all, in the long run, to thrive.
